passage: Sports day was so loud that nobody could hear anything. Tenzin crossed the line first in the relay, and his teammate Binita jumped up with her palm raised. He slapped it in a high-five, both laughing. The chief guest came down to the track and held out a hand. “Well run.” Tenzin shook it, politely, looking her in the eye. Then he saw Binita standing a little apart. She didn't like being touched by strangers. When another teammate held up a hand to her, she gave a big wave instead. The teammate waved back, grinning, and the noise closed over all of them.

qa.q: Who crossed the line first in the relay?
qa.a: Tenzin crossed the line first.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he slapped Binita's high-five, and what did the handshake show?
qa.a: He was probably excited and proud of his run. The handshake with the chief guest showed politeness and respect, in a more formal moment.

qa.q: What could Binita do when she prefers not to touch someone?
qa.a: Offer a wave instead, as she did, which still shows warmth.

qa.q: How might the other teammate feel when Binita waves rather than high-fives?
qa.a: Probably fine with it, since the teammate waved back grinning. The teammate may see the wave as a friendly greeting in its own right.

grounding: High-five, handshake and a wave each carry warmth; a child who prefers not to touch can wave.

passage:
At the school gate in the morning, Shankar held out a fist and Lokesh bumped it. “Ready for the test?” “Nope,” said Lokesh. “But ready for lunch.” They grinned.
Inside, the visiting principal stood in the corridor, and Shankar stepped forward to shake her hand. “Good morning, ma'am. Welcome to our school.” She smiled. Lokesh hung back. He was shy about touch with people he didn't know, so he joined his palms and said, “Namaste, ma'am.”
She returned the namaste. “Lovely to meet you.” Lokesh let out a breath.

qa.q: What did Lokesh say when Shankar asked if he was ready for the test?
qa.a: He said, “Nope. But ready for lunch.”

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when he hung back, and what did he do about it?
qa.a: He was shy about touching someone he did not know, so he chose a namaste instead of a handshake. He seemed relieved when she returned it.

qa.q: What does this show about greeting choices?
qa.a: A child can pick a warm, respectful greeting that suits him, such as a namaste, wave or fist bump, and that is enough.

qa.q: How might the visiting principal see Lokesh's namaste?
qa.a: As a polite and warm greeting, since she returned it and said it was lovely to meet him.

grounding: Fist bump, handshake and namaste all show warmth; a child who prefers not to touch can offer another greeting.

passage: “We won! Madhuri, we WON!” Rashmi flung a hand up for a high-five. Madhuri stepped back and waved instead, both hands, grinning. “Yes! Best relay ever!” Rashmi's hand hung in the air. “Oh. You don't do high-fives?” “Not really. I don't love touching, even with friends. But I'm SO happy.” “Okay.” Rashmi lowered the hand, then waved back wildly with both arms. “Double wave!” Madhuri laughed. “Double wave is perfect.” Their coach, jogging up, held out a fist for a bump, looked at Madhuri and switched to a thumbs-up. “Great running, you two.”

qa.q: What had Rashmi and Madhuri just won?
qa.a: They had just won the relay.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when the hand hung in the air?
qa.a: Rashmi felt a moment of surprise and awkwardness, unsure whether Madhuri shared the joy.

qa.q: Which choice worked for both of them, and why?
qa.a: The double wave worked, because it let them celebrate warmly without touch Madhuri didn't want 🙌

qa.q: What does Madhuri's wave show about Madhuri's feelings?
qa.a: Madhuri was just as happy about the win and simply prefers not to touch, even with friends.

grounding: Shows a high-five offered to celebrate, and a child who prefers not to touch offering a wave instead.

passage: I'm Vijay. On prize day last year, the chief guest held out her hand for a handshake, and I was so excited I bumped it with my fist instead. She blinked, then laughed and bumped back. My friend Gargi nearly fell off her chair. Afterwards she explained, like a teacher: “High-five is for winning something with your mates. Fist bump is for saying hi to friends. Handshake is for being polite to grown-ups you don't know.” I made her practise all three with me behind the stage. Now I think about who's in front of me before my hand moves. The chief guest didn't mind, though.

qa.q: What did the chief guest hold out on prize day?
qa.a: The chief guest held out her hand for a handshake.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when the fist bump happened?
qa.a: Vijay was so excited that the fist bump came out by mistake, and afterwards felt a bit embarrassed and amused.

qa.q: What did Gargi teach Vijay, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She explained when to use a high-five, a fist bump and a handshake, so Vijay can choose the right greeting for each person.

qa.q: How did the chief guest react to the fist bump?
qa.a: She blinked in surprise, then laughed and bumped back, taking it as warmth rather than rudeness.

grounding: Shows a child learning when a high-five, fist bump or handshake fits, as quick touches that carry warmth and respect.

passage: Class note, Monday. Harish, Class 2. Our door-greeting chart is working well. Each morning the children point to high-five, fist bump, handshake or wave, and I match it. Most choose high-fives; the slap is half the fun. Damini always points to the wave. Today Ansh said, “Why are you so boring? Just high-five!” Damini's hand hovered near the chart, then dropped. I said, “Waves count just as much in this class,” and waved at her with both hands, big and silly. She giggled and waved back. At home time she chose the wave again, standing a bit taller. Tomorrow I'll remind the class that every greeting on the chart is a good one.

qa.q: Which greeting does Damini always choose?
qa.a: Damini always points to the wave.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when her hand hovered and dropped?
qa.a: Damini felt unsure and a little embarrassed after being called boring, wondering whether to change her choice.

qa.q: How did Harish support Damini's choice?
qa.a: Harish said waves count just as much and gave her a big, silly wave, showing her choice was welcome.

qa.q: How did Ansh see Damini's wave?
qa.a: Ansh saw it as boring compared with high-fives, not realising some children prefer not to touch.

grounding: Shows children choosing high-fives, fist bumps or handshakes as warm greetings, and a child who prefers not to touch choosing a wave.

passage:
Saturday

WE WON the inter-school quiz! 🎉 When they called our name, I high-fived Aman so hard my palm stung. Then the chief guest shook all our hands, very serious, like we were grown-ups.

I held out my hand to Noor for a high-five too, but she just smiled and waved. I felt a bit silly with my hand hanging there. On the bus I asked if she was cross with me. She said no, she just doesn't like touching much, even with friends, and waving is how she does it. So we made up a secret wave: two wiggly fingers and a salute. Aman wants a fist-bump version.

Vijay

qa.q: What did the chief guest do?
qa.a: The chief guest shook all their hands, very seriously.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel with a hand hanging in the air?
qa.a: A bit silly and unsure, wondering whether Noor was cross.

qa.q: What did Vijay do that fixed the awkward moment?
qa.a: Vijay asked Noor on the bus instead of assuming, and then they made up a secret wave together.

qa.q: How does Noor prefer to celebrate with friends, and why?
qa.a: Noor prefers a wave because she doesn't like touching much, even with friends; it has nothing to do with being cross.

grounding: It is a child's diary about high-fives, handshakes and fist bumps as warm quick touches, and a friend who prefers a wave instead.
